title: The Lock That Lost Quorum
summary: A ride-hailing app uses ZooKeeper so no driver gets two riders. Someone ran it with 2 nodes to save money.
scenario: 6,000 requests per second: riders polling for cars, and drivers accepting trips. Each acceptance takes a ZooKeeper lock on the driver so they can't be assigned twice.
To cut costs, the ZooKeeper ensemble was shrunk to 2 nodes. "We still have a spare," the reasoning went.
Last night one ZooKeeper node restarted and every trip assignment in the city failed until it came back. Make coordination survive a node failure, within budget.

objectives.label: No unsafe contended writes (no double bookings)

hints: Run the simulation and open Single points of failure. Why is a component with 2 replicas listed?
ZooKeeper only works while a majority of its nodes agree. With 2 nodes, the majority is 2, so losing either one stops it.
Majority of 3 is 2, so a 3-node ensemble survives one failure. 4 nodes still only survives one (majority is 3), so it costs more for nothing. Set ZooKeeper to 3 replicas.
explanation: Consensus systems (ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul) need a strict majority, a quorum, to make progress. That rule is what prevents split-brain, where two halves of a cluster each think they are in charge.
Fault tolerance is floor((n − 1) / 2): 1 node tolerates 0 failures, 2 tolerate 0, 3 tolerate 1, 4 tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2. That's why ensembles are always odd-sized.
A 2-node ensemble is strictly worse than 1: twice the cost, twice the chance that some node is down, and the same zero fault tolerance.

ZooKeeper locks use ephemeral sequential znodes. If the holder's session dies, its znode vanishes and the next waiter is notified. That makes them safer than lease-based Redis locks for long critical sections, at the cost of latency.
